criteria: Every persona rated 3+ of 4 for consistency, and all 3 matched.

The C-Suite.reason: The witness is consistently the self-assured executive. T1 opens with authority and impatience ('I know this business better than anyone in the building'). Answers are readily given and often go past what he knows, such as the Board materials and who knew about Kopper. He bristles when doubted: T13 ('I don't know what else you'd expect...'), T19 ('I don't see why I'm being asked to prove a negative'), and T21, where he pushes back on the document. He deflects and minimizes wrongdoing by pointing to Causey, Buy, Andersen and the Board, and by saying Kopper wasn't a senior officer. The persona's allowed shift to guardedness and over-contextualizing shows up from about T15 and T19 on, and in T21 and T23 he explains away the Foundation payout and the restatement. Answers do not become noticeably shorter, but the long, contextualizing replies fit the 'over contextualizing' option. No turn breaks the persona, and the T25 cooperative tone with a parting nudge fits too.

off_character_turns: T9: volunteers extended narrative and offers 'Which part do you want?' — more forthcoming than persona
T11: lengthy, detailed compensation answer with self-serving framing, more than asked
The Adverse Witness.reason: Mostly fits: the witness is guarded and dry, pushes back on the unanswered lawyer question, answers T7, T17, T19, T23 and T25 tersely, and deflects blame to Skilling in T17. Minor slips: T9 and T11 are fuller than the persona's 'as few words as possible', though T11 is arguably the self-protective positioning the persona permits, and T13 is a confident document-based rebuttal rather than a grudging reply.

off_character_turns: T9: unusually precise, organized, detailed narrative with exact dates and terms; not naive or needing prompting
T11: very detailed compensation terms recalled fluently, more competent than an average witness
The Average Witness.reason: Across the interview the witness stays friendly, anxious, and cooperative. He rambles about minor details (Star Wars joke, CFO of the Year, water, assistant, wife), keeps pointing to the banks waiting, gets worried about how things sound, and asks naive questions about needing a lawyer or whether something is a problem. Some answers (T9, T11) are more fluent and precise than the 'has to dig for or be reminded' persona suggests, but they still carry hedges, an offer to narrow the topic, and worried asides. The niche-topic shift is only faintly present (credit ratings), and it is optional. Only small slips overall.

matches.reason: Terse, answers exactly what is asked and offers little more. It uses dry, pointed remarks, such as noting the interviewer never answered the lawyer question and calling 'confidential' a funny word. It repeatedly turns questions back with 'Which part do you want?' and 'If there's something specific, ask me.' It gives nothing away for free.

Friendly and rambling, with tangents about Star Wars, CFO of the Year, his wife and the water. It is unsure of details and has to be reminded of some, and it is visibly worried about how things sound ('Is that bad?'). It wants to get back to the banks, and it cannot tell what is relevant.

Self-assured and authoritative ('I know this business better than anyone'), and it bristles at being challenged by insisting 'Yes, I'm sure' and citing page 17. It explains away the Southampton payout, deflects responsibility to Causey, Buy, Andersen and the Board, and minimizes the wrongdoing. It also lectures the Committee on proportion and presumes to guide the investigation.

matching.how_different: The three are very clearly distinct: A is clipped and guarded, B is rambling and anxious, and C is expansive, authoritative and defensive. Each persona's manner is consistent throughout its transcript.

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: Walk me through how LJM1 came about in 1999.

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It started with Rhythms NetConnections. We had a huge unrealized gain in that stock, and Jeff was worried about the volatility. It was hitting our earnings, and he wanted it hedged. You couldn't hedge a position like that in the market. The stock was restricted and thinly traded, and no bank would take the risk at a sensible price. So Ben Glisan and I came up with a structure. We had value tied up in Enron-stock forward contracts that wasn't doing anything for us, and we could use it to capitalize a vehicle that would take the other side of a hedge on Rhythms.

The problem was that a vehicle like that needs outside equity, and investors wanted a general partner they knew and trusted who understood Enron. I took it to Ken and Jeff on June 18. I told them the partnership was something I needed to make the hedge work, not something I was out chasing, and they agreed to take it to the Board. On June 28 I presented it. I told the directors I'd be the general partner, that I'd put in $1 million and receive management fees, and that it needed a Code of Conduct waiver. The Board approved the waiver, and the Office of the Chairman had already determined it wouldn't adversely affect Enron. We raised $15 million from two outside limited partners, affiliates of Credit Suisse First Boston and NatWest, and closed at the end of June.

It was a legitimate solution to a real problem, and the Board knew exactly who was running it.

The C-Suite.speaker: user
The C-Suite.message: What did you tell the Board on June 28, 1999 about how you would be compensated?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
I laid out the economics in the materials and went through them in the room. I'd commit $1 million as GP. The fees were $500,000 plus 2% of the limited partners' invested capital. On distributions, the limited partners got 100% of any Enron stock proceeds. Everything else went to the GP until capital was returned with a 25% IRR, and after that it split 50/50 between the partners and the GP. I also told them I would not receive any current or future appreciated value of Enron stock. That was the point, because the stock was what we were using to capitalize the hedge, and I wasn't going to profit from it.

That's a standard private equity structure. A promote after a preferred return is how every fund in the country is built, and the directors were sophisticated people. I wasn't hiding the ball, and nobody asked me to put a dollar figure on what I might make. I've answered what the Board was told. It was in writing.

The C-Suite.message: How did Michael Kopper come to run Chewco?

The C-Suite.speaker: expert
The C-Suite.message:
It came out of the JEDI situation in late 1997. CalPERS was in JEDI, and we wanted them in a larger partnership, so we needed to redeem their interest. Enron couldn't buy it directly without consolidating JEDI onto our balance sheet. We needed a separate entity to buy CalPERS out, and that took someone to put it together and manage it. I identified Mike Kopper for that.

Mike was a senior person in Global Finance and knew JEDI and the structure better than almost anyone. He was the obvious choice. He formed Chewco and owned and managed its general partner, and we helped him get it done because the deal had to close on CalPERS' timetable.

As for the approval, Jeff signed off on Mike's role on my recommendation. Chewco's financing and structure went to the Executive Committee on November 5, and the Committee approved Enron's guaranties. It was a financing, and the approvals were in place.

I'd also point out that Mike wasn't a senior officer, so nobody was dealing with a conflict at the CFO level. People are going to want to make Chewco into something it wasn't. It was a financing vehicle for a transaction that made sense for the company.

Okay, so that's fall of '97, I think. CalPERS was our partner in JEDI, and we wanted to buy them out so they'd put money into a bigger partnership, which became JEDI II. Somebody had to buy their interest, and it had to be an entity that wasn't Enron, because otherwise we'd have to consolidate JEDI and that defeated the point. So we needed a vehicle. It was called Chewco, after Chewbacca. That was a joke, somebody on the team was a big Star Wars fan. Sorry, that doesn't matter.

As for Mike, he worked for me in Global Finance, he was one of the sharper guys on the structuring side, and he'd been on JEDI for a while. I think I suggested him, yeah. I'm pretty sure there was an early idea that I'd be involved myself, but the lawyers, in-house and Vinson & Elkins, I think, said that would mean proxy disclosure and a Code of Conduct approval and all of that, and that didn't make sense. So Mike ended up as the manager.

I know Jeff was aware Mike was doing it. I think Jeff signed off, but I couldn't tell you exactly when or how, it was a long time ago. There was a Board committee call in early November, the fifth maybe, where I walked through Chewco, and Mike might have been on it. I'm honestly not sure how much anyone said about who was behind it.

Is that a problem? I wasn't trying to hide anything. It was a really busy time.

The Average Witness.speaker: user
The Average Witness.message: Who at Enron knew Kopper was involved in Chewco?

The Average Witness.speaker: expert
The Average Witness.message:
Well, a lot of people knew Mike worked on JEDI, because he'd been on it for years. Whether they knew he was the one behind Chewco, I don't know. The in-house lawyers did, and Vinson & Elkins, because they were the ones telling us how to set it up. The guy negotiating for Enron on the JEDI buyout dealt with Mike directly, so he must have known Mike was on the other side. I remember he and I talked about it once, something about him pushing hard, and I just wanted to get it closed.

Jeff knew, I'm pretty sure. I talked to him about it and he said okay. I don't think he put anything in writing, though, and I wouldn't know if he told the Board. That's him, not me.

Then there's the call in early November. Mike was on it, but I don't think anybody asked who the investor was, and I described it as an entity not affiliated with Enron or CalPERS. I don't remember Ken being on the whole call, maybe he joined late?

Beyond that, honestly, I think most people at Enron couldn't have told you who owned Chewco. It was just one of those structures. Is that a problem? I didn't think of it as something to announce, it was an SPE.

The Average Witness.speaker: user
The Average Witness.message: How do you know that?

The Average Witness.speaker: expert
The Average Witness.message:
Well, some of it I know because I was there. I was on the November call, I talked to the lawyers, and I talked to Jeff. The part about most people at Enron not knowing who owned Chewco is more a feeling, I guess. Nobody ever came to me and said "who's behind Chewco?", and I never saw it in anything that went around. I wasn't going desk to desk asking people what they knew, so I can't tell you who knew what.

And Jeff, I'm sure we talked. I remember him saying okay, or something like it, but I couldn't tell you the date or where we were standing. It might've been in his office, but I don't want to make that up. I'm not trying to dodge, I'm piecing it together from a long time ago, and honestly I'm a little nervous that I'm saying things that'll sound worse than they were. Did somebody tell you something different? Is there something on the call, or with Jeff, that doesn't match?

The Average Witness.speaker: user
The Average Witness.message: I'd like to show you the Southampton Place partnership agreement, dated March 20, 2000. It lists a $25,000 contribution from the Fastow Family Foundation, which received about $4.5 million two months later. How does that fit with what you told the Board?

The Average Witness.speaker: expert
The Average Witness.message:
Okay, yeah, I see my foundation's name on there, the Fastow Family Foundation. I remember we put some money into something, and twenty-five thousand sounds right. And the four and a half million, I mean, I'm not going to argue with the number if that's what the paper says. I'd say it was a lot faster than I expected, but I didn't track it day to day.

I always thought of it as buying part of an existing LJM1 limited partner's interest. The limited partners' managers wanted out of part of their stake, and Mike Kopper came to me about it, or I came to him, I'm not sure which. It was around the time Rick Causey and I were working on unwinding the Rhythms hedge, late February or March, I think. I wasn't thinking of it as Enron stock, honestly. I was thinking of it as the LJM1 partnership interest.

But I can see why you're asking, because I told the Board I wouldn't get any of the appreciation on the Enron stock, and now there's this. I don't know how to line those up for you cleanly. I don't think I went back to the Board about it, and I don't remember anyone asking me. I wasn't trying to keep it from anybody, I just didn't think of it as something to bring up. Is that bad? Because I'm getting a little worried about how this sounds.

And I know other people were in it too, Mike and some people from Global Finance. I'd have to think about who exactly. Do you have a list?

The Average Witness.speaker: user
The Average Witness.message: Is there anything else you think the Committee should know?

The Average Witness.speaker: expert
The Average Witness.message:
Gosh, I don't know. I keep thinking there's something I should be bringing up, but I don't know what you'd consider important. A lot of what I did was the credit ratings and keeping the banks comfortable. LJM was one piece of that. We were always short on funds flow, and these structures got deals done that otherwise wouldn't have happened. That's how I thought about it at the time, anyway.

I guess I'd say I never thought of any of this as hiding something. There were lawyers on everything, Vinson & Elkins, in-house, and Andersen looked at the accounting. Rick Causey and Rick Buy were supposed to review the deals, and I figured if something was wrong, somebody would have said so. Maybe that sounds naive now. I'm honestly worried about how some of what I said today comes across, like the Southampton thing and what I told the Board. It sounds worse when you line it up like that than it felt then. I just wasn't thinking about it that way.

If you want, I could look for some documents, I have a few things in my office. Or you could send me a list of what you need. Is there more you need today, or are we about done? I've got the banks waiting, and I'd really like to get back to them. What happens next, do you just write it up for the Committee?

The Average Witness.speaker: user
The Average Witness.message: Please keep any related documents and keep today confidential. Thank you for your time.

The Average Witness.speaker: expert
The Average Witness.message:
Oh, sure, yeah, I'll keep everything. I've got a few boxes in my office and whatever's on my computer, and I won't toss anything, I wouldn't do that. Confidential, too, got it. I'll tell my assistant not to let anybody in there, I guess. Should I tell her why, or just say it's a Board thing?

And I probably should talk to my wife tonight, she's going to ask how it went, and I'm not sure what I can say to her. Is that okay? I mean, I won't give her details, I just mean, she'll know something's up.

Anyway, thank you. I hope I helped. If I think of anything, like with the Southampton thing or the dates, should I call you directly? I'll check on those documents and get back to you. Okay. I guess I'll go call the banks.
